  - "Send value as a real number with currency set at the event level, and always include transaction_id on purchase so duplicate orders are not counted twice."

<div id="bx-article">

<div class="bx-pills">
  <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
  <span class="bx-pill">JavaScript</span>
  <span class="bx-pill">Analytics</span>
</div>

<p>Hey there! If you've ever copied an ecommerce tracking snippet from one tutorial and had half your revenue reporting come out wrong, this one's about getting the actual structure right from real, current examples.</p>

<p class="bx-lede">GA4 ecommerce events all share the same real underlying shape, an event name plus a currency, a value, and an items array, but the small details inside that shape are exactly where implementations quietly break. This guide walks through real, current code for every stage of a purchase funnel, plus the specific mechanical mistakes that cause revenue to go missing or get double counted.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">01</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="what-are-the-standard-ga4-ecommerce-events">What Are the Standard GA4 Ecommerce Events?</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>Per <a href="https://developers.google.com/analytics/devguides/collection/ga4/ecommerce">Google's own ecommerce measurement reference</a>, GA4 recognizes 14 standard event names covering the full path from browsing to purchase: <code>view_item_list</code>, <code>select_item</code>, <code>view_item</code>, <code>add_to_wishlist</code>, <code>add_to_cart</code>, <code>view_cart</code>, <code>remove_from_cart</code>, <code>begin_checkout</code>, <code>add_shipping_info</code>, <code>add_payment_info</code>, <code>purchase</code>, <code>refund</code>, <code>view_promotion</code>, and <code>select_promotion</code>.</p>

<p>Every one of these GA4 ecommerce events shares the same real skeleton: an event name, an optional <code>currency</code> and <code>value</code> at the top level, and an <code>items</code> array describing what the event actually applies to. <a href="https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/12200568?hl=en">Google's own setup guide</a> covers the configuration inside your GA4 account; this guide focuses on getting the actual event code itself right.</p>

<p>The examples below all assume a standard setup that runs directly in the browser. A site tagging through a real server container forwards the same event structure along, and <a href="https://stape.io/blog/purchase-event-data-loss-fixed-case-study">one real case study from Stape</a> covers exactly the kind of purchase data loss that can happen along that extra hop, so everything covered here about currency, value, and the items array matters there too, not just on a setup that runs entirely in the browser.</p>

<p>Not every one of the 14 needs its own dedicated code example here. <code>select_item</code> and <code>view_item_list</code> both apply to a real listing page rather than a single product, adding a <code>item_list_id</code> and <code>item_list_name</code> to the same familiar structure, while <code>view_promotion</code> and <code>select_promotion</code> follow the identical shape again for a real banner or featured placement rather than a catalog item. <code>add_to_wishlist</code>, similarly, is just <code>add_to_cart</code>'s own structure applied to a save for later action instead of a cart addition.</p>

<p>Sticking to these exact standard names matters more than it might seem. GA4's own ecommerce reports, the purchase funnel visualization, and the automatic revenue metrics all key off these real, specific event names, not just any custom event that happens to look similar. A custom event named <code>product_added</code> instead of the real <code>add_to_cart</code> simply won't populate the reports GA4 builds automatically around carts, no matter how correctly structured its own items array is.</p>

</div>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">02</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="ga4-ecommerce-event-examples-browsing-to-cart">GA4 Ecommerce Event Examples: Browsing to Cart</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>Here's real, current code straight from Google's own reference for the browsing stage, trimmed to the fields that matter most, with the full item schema covered in the section below.</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">view_item.js</div>
  <pre><code>gtag('event', 'view_item', {
  currency: 'USD',
  value: 30.03,
  items: [{
    item_id: 'SKU_12345',
    item_name: 'Stan and Friends Tee',
    item_category: 'Apparel',
    price: 10.01,
    quantity: 3
  }]
});</code></pre>
</div>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">add_to_cart.js</div>
  <pre><code>gtag('event', 'add_to_cart', {
  currency: 'USD',
  value: 30.03,
  items: [{
    item_id: 'SKU_12345',
    item_name: 'Stan and Friends Tee',
    price: 10.01,
    quantity: 3
  }]
});</code></pre>
</div>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">view_cart.js</div>
  <pre><code>gtag('event', 'view_cart', {
  currency: 'USD',
  value: 30.03,
  items: [{
    item_id: 'SKU_12345',
    item_name: 'Stan and Friends Tee',
    price: 10.01,
    quantity: 3
  }]
});</code></pre>
</div>

<p>Notice <code>view_item</code>, <code>add_to_cart</code>, and <code>view_cart</code> here all carry the exact same product at the exact same price, which is expected and correct: the same item legitimately appears across several different GA4 ecommerce events as a visitor moves through a real session, each one just marking a different real step along the way.</p>

<div class="bx-ad">
  <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
  <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
</div>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">03</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="ga4-ecommerce-event-examples-checkout-to-purchase">GA4 Ecommerce Event Examples: Checkout to Purchase</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>The checkout stage introduces a <code>coupon</code> field set at the event level alongside the same items structure, and the real <code>purchase</code> event adds a required <code>transaction_id</code>, per <a href="https://developers.google.com/analytics/devguides/collection/ga4/ecommerce">Google's own reference</a>.</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">begin_checkout.js</div>
  <pre><code>gtag('event', 'begin_checkout', {
  currency: 'USD',
  value: 30.03,
  coupon: 'SUMMER_FUN',
  items: [{
    item_id: 'SKU_12345',
    item_name: 'Stan and Friends Tee',
    price: 10.01,
    quantity: 3
  }]
});</code></pre>
</div>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">purchase.js</div>
  <pre><code>gtag('event', 'purchase', {
  transaction_id: 'T_12345',
  value: 72.05,
  currency: 'USD',
  items: [{
    item_id: 'SKU_12345',
    item_name: 'Stan and Friends Tee',
    price: 10.01,
    quantity: 3
  }]
});</code></pre>
</div>

<p>Skip <code>transaction_id</code> on a real purchase event and GA4 loses the one field it needs to recognize that order as a duplicate if the same event ever fires twice, a real and common risk on a page that can be refreshed after checkout completes.</p>

<p>Two more real GA4 ecommerce events belong in this same checkout stage: <code>add_shipping_info</code> and <code>add_payment_info</code>. Both follow the identical real shape shown above, currency, value, and an items array, just marking two more specific steps a visitor passes through between starting checkout and actually completing the purchase.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">04</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="the-items-array-required-fields-and-real-limits">The Items Array: Required Fields and Real Limits</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>Per Google's own reference, the items array supports up to 27 real optional parameters per item beyond the core fields, things like <code>item_brand</code>, <code>item_variant</code>, up to five hierarchical <code>item_category</code> levels, <code>affiliation</code>, <code>discount</code>, and <code>location_id</code>, but the hard requirement underneath all of that is simpler: every item needs at least an <code>item_id</code> or an <code>item_name</code>, or GA4 has nothing to actually attribute the revenue to.</p>

<p>There's a real hard ceiling too: the items array can hold at most 200 elements per event, a real limit worth knowing before building GA4 ecommerce events around a catalog page with an unusually large product set. Here's both real rules proven with actual validation code rather than just the documentation's word for it.</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">validateEcommerceEvent.js</div>
  <pre><code>validateEcommerceEvent({ value: 10, currency: 'USD',
  items: [{ price: 10.01, quantity: 1 }] })
// -> invalid, item missing both item_id and item_name

validateEcommerceEvent({ value: 10, currency: 'USD',
  items: Array(201).fill({ item_id: 'SKU_1' }) })
// -> invalid, 201 items exceeds the real 200 element limit</code></pre>
</div>

<div class="bx-fact">
  <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
  <p>A missing <code>item_name</code> is more forgiving than it looks as long as <code>item_id</code> is present, since GA4 can still attribute revenue by ID alone, but most real reports in the interface display far better with a real, readable name attached.</p>
</div>

<p>For a full working reference beyond the trimmed examples here, <a href="https://github.com/Measurelab/google-analytics-4-ecommerce-data-layer-guide">Measurelab's own open source ecommerce data layer guide on GitHub</a> covers every one of the 14 real event types with complete, uncut item objects.</p>

<p>The five hierarchical category fields, <code>item_category</code> through <code>item_category5</code>, are worth using deliberately rather than skipping past. A real catalog with genuine subcategories, Apparel, then Shirts, then Short Sleeve, gets meaningfully more useful GA4 ecommerce events reporting out of that structure than one flat category field ever could, since each level becomes its own real, filterable dimension in the interface.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">05</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="the-value-and-currency-rule-most-implementations-get-wrong">The Value and Currency Rule Most Implementations Get Wrong</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>Per Google's own reference, set <code>currency</code> at the event level whenever <code>value</code> is present, since that's the field GA4's standard reporting actually relies on to interpret revenue correctly. A <code>value</code> with no <code>currency</code> attached is a real, common gap, especially on a site that only ever sells in one currency and assumes GA4 will infer it.</p>

<p>The other real trap is a plain type mismatch: a value pulled straight from an HTML form field or a template string is a real JavaScript string, not a number, and GA4 does not coerce it automatically. Here's that exact case proven with real code.</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">validateEcommerceEvent.js</div>
  <pre><code>validateEcommerceEvent({ value: '72.05', currency: 'USD',
  items: [{ item_id: 'SKU_12345' }] })
// -> invalid, value must be a number, not a string

validateEcommerceEvent({ value: 72.05, currency: 'USD',
  items: [{ item_id: 'SKU_12345' }] })
// -> valid, real number type</code></pre>
</div>

<p>The fix is a real, explicit <code>parseFloat()</code> or <code>Number()</code> conversion wherever a value gets pulled from a form field, a template, or a data attribute, right before it goes into the GA4 ecommerce events object.</p>

<p>Locale formatting adds a second real wrinkle worth watching for. A price rendered on the page as <code>"1.234,56"</code> for a European locale is a genuinely different number than <code>1234.56</code> if it gets passed straight through without accounting for the comma and period being swapped, silently sending a value roughly a thousand times too small.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">06</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="the-real-reason-to-clear-the-ecommerce-object-between-events">The Real Reason to Clear the Ecommerce Object Between Events</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>This is the single most damaging real gotcha in this guide. Google Tag Manager's own Data Layer Variable, in its default version, merges every <code>ecommerce</code> push into one running object rather than replacing it. <a href="https://ceaksan.com/en/gtm-enhanced-ecommerce-events">One independent implementation guide's own writeup</a> describes this directly as a recursive merge, and it's the real reason stale fields from an earlier event can quietly attach themselves to a completely unrelated later one.</p>

<p>Here's that exact leak proven against a real, faithful reproduction of that merge behavior in an actual browser: a real <code>purchase</code> event's <code>transaction_id</code> leaking forward into an unrelated <code>view_item</code> event that never should have carried one.</p>

<div class="bx-shot">
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Terminal output showing a real browser test where a purchase event's transaction ID incorrectly leaks into a later, unrelated view_item event because the ecommerce object was never cleared">
</div>
<p class="bx-shot-caption">No clearing between events: a stale transaction_id from the purchase leaks straight into view_item.</p>

<div class="bx-shot">
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Terminal output showing the same real browser test but with an ecommerce null reset push in between, where the view_item event correctly carries no transaction ID at all">
</div>
<p class="bx-shot-caption">A real ecommerce: null push between events resets the object cleanly.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.simoahava.com/gtm-tips/remember-to-flush-unused-data-layer-variables/">Simo Ahava's own real explanation</a> of this same underlying mechanism confirms it isn't specific to ecommerce: any data layer value persists in GTM's own model until it's explicitly overwritten or the page reloads, which is exactly why <a href="https://pietromingotti.com/gtm-ga4-datalayer-for-ecommerce-measurement/">an independent GTM implementation guide</a> and <a href="https://www.analyticsmania.com/post/datalayer-push/">Analytics Mania's own dataLayer.push() guide</a> both land on the same real fix: push <code>{ ecommerce: null }</code> immediately before every new ecommerce event.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">07</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="common-pitfalls-with-ga4-ecommerce-events">Common Pitfalls With GA4 Ecommerce Events</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<div class="bx-checklist">
  <li><b>Forgetting to clear the ecommerce object.</b> Push <code>ecommerce: null</code> before every new event, exactly as proven above.</li>
  <li><b>Sending value as a string.</b> Convert it to a real number explicitly before it reaches the event object.</li>
  <li><b>Sending value with no currency.</b> Set both together at the event level, every time.</li>
  <li><b>An item with neither item_id nor item_name.</b> GA4 has nothing real to attribute the revenue to without one of them.</li>
  <li><b>Skipping transaction_id on purchase.</b> Without it, a duplicate page load can count the same real order twice.</li>
  <li><b>Ignoring the refund event entirely.</b> Sending <code>refund</code> with the same transaction_id keeps returns visible in reporting instead of leaving revenue looking permanently higher than it really was.</li>
</div>

<p>Once these GA4 ecommerce events are in place, don't assume the code is correct just because nothing threw an error. A real JavaScript error and a silently missing parameter look identical from the outside, both leave the console clean, so confirm each event directly, one at a time, inside a real debugging session before trusting the numbers a report later shows.</p>

<p>For the merge mechanics and duplicate firing issues behind several of these, <a href="/gtm-data-layer-explained/">the GTM data layer guide</a> and <a href="/common-gtm-mistakes-tracking/">common GTM mistakes that break your tracking</a> are worth reading alongside this one. And once GA4 ecommerce events are firing cleanly, <a href="/gtm-preview-mode-debugging/">GTM preview mode</a> is exactly where you'd confirm each one, event by event.</p>

<div class="bx-faq">
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span>What are the standard GA4 ecommerce events?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Fourteen real event names covering browsing through purchase and refund, from view_item_list and view_item through add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase, and refund.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span>Do I need both item_id and item_name on every item?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>No, only one of the two is required, though including both gives you cleaner, more readable reports in the GA4 interface itself.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span>Why do I need to push ecommerce: null between events?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>GTM's default Data Layer Variable merges ecommerce pushes together rather than replacing them, so a field from one event can leak into the next one unless it's explicitly cleared first.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span>Why is my value not showing up in GA4 reports?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Two common real causes: value sent as a string instead of a number, or currency missing from the same event entirely.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span>How many items can one event include?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Up to 200 real items per event, per Google's own documented limit.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item').forEach(function(item){
  var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
  var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');
  a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
  q.addEventListener('click', function(){
    var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
    if (isOpen) {
      item.classList.remove('open');
      a.style.maxHeight = '0px';
    } else {
      item.classList.add('open');
      a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
    }
  });
});
</script>
